issues.legal_issue: Under the applicable customary law, a daughter’s sons inherit non-ancestral property that devolved on their mother, in preference to her father’s collaterals, and a gift by the daughter to those sons accelerates their succession.
material_facts: The property had been found to be non-ancestral and had devolved by inheritance on the daughter.
The daughter had sons and gifted the disputed property to them.
The plaintiffs claimed as the deceased owner’s collaterals and sought to preserve reversionary rights.
issues.conclusion: The daughter’s sons were the nearest heirs under the applicable custom and excluded the collaterals; the gift to them accelerated succession, so the plaintiffs were no longer reversioners.
issues.legal_principle: Rattigan’s Digest of Customary Law, paragraph 23(2), states that a daughter is preferred to collaterals in respect of her father’s acquired property. The court relied on the description of customary succession in Roe and Rattigan’s Tribal Law of the Punjab, as quoted in Rattigan’s Digest, and on Lehna v. Mst. Thakri and Lal Singh v. Roor Singh. Under the custom applicable to the parties, a daughter who succeeds to non-ancestral property holds it as a means of passing it to her sons and their male descendants, who exclude the collaterals. A transfer to those next heirs can operate as an acceleration of succession, irrespective of the form of the transfer.

predicates.customary_succession_dispute: The dispute concerns succession under a custom governing the parties.
predicates.daughter_succeeded_to_nonancestral_prope: A daughter inherited property that was treated as non-ancestral.
predicates.daughter_had_sons: The daughter had sons who could take the property through her line.
predicates.applicable_custom_recognizes_daughters_l: The custom governing succession treats the daughter’s sons as entitled to follow her in the property.

issues.definition: When a customary succession dispute concerns non-ancestral property inherited by a daughter who has sons, and the applicable custom recognizes her line, the daughter’s line takes precedence over collaterals and a transfer to the sons accelerates succession.

issues.legal_issue: Omission of a small portion of the property from an otherwise bona fide surrender does not invalidate the surrender or prevent acceleration of succession.
material_facts: The daughter gave away the property subject to the surrender, while retaining a house that formed only a very small part of the estate.
The retained dwelling was small, and the daughter’s sons already lived there with her.
The gift also included property that the daughter had an absolute right to give, supporting the finding that she intended to efface herself from the estate.
issues.conclusion: The retention of the small house did not invalidate the surrender, and the gift operated to accelerate succession.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the surrender principle stated in Mulla’s Hindu Law, 11th edition, page 217: omission, through ignorance or oversight, of a small part of the property does not affect a surrender’s validity when the surrender is otherwise bona fide. The court found the small retained house, in the circumstances, did not show an intention to retain the estate.

predicates.surrender_dispute_in_succession_case: The dispute concerns whether a surrender in a succession matter was effective.
predicates.omitted_property_was_small: The person making the surrender retained only a small portion of the property.
predicates.surrender_was_otherwise_bona_fide: The circumstances show that the person otherwise intended bona fide to relinquish the estate.

issues.definition: When a succession dispute concerns a surrender, a small omission does not invalidate it if the surrender was otherwise bona fide.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent finding on the non-ancestral character of property is not reopened on appeal where the issue was conceded below and the admitted facts cannot be separated from the legal conclusion.
material_facts: The lower courts had concurrently found that the property was non-ancestral.
The appellant’s counsel had conceded that point in the courts below.
The finding involved a mixed question of law and fact, and the admitted facts were not shown to be separable from the legal conclusion.
Earlier judgments between the parties or their predecessors had also determined that the property was non-ancestral.
issues.conclusion: The court did not allow the appellant to reopen the finding and accepted that the property was non-ancestral.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the character of the property as a mixed question of law and fact that could not be reconsidered on the basis proposed once the relevant point had been conceded and the admitted facts could not be disentangled from the legal conclusion. It also observed that the earlier judgments determining the property’s character were res judicata.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and finding_was_concurrent and issue_was_mixed_law_and_fact and appellant_conceded_issue_below and prior_judgments_determined_the_issue

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.finding_was_concurrent: The courts below had reached the same finding on the issue.
predicates.issue_was_mixed_law_and_fact: The issue depended on both facts and the legal conclusion drawn from them, and those elements could not be separated on the record presented.
predicates.appellant_conceded_issue_below: The appellant’s counsel accepted the issue in the courts below.
predicates.prior_judgments_determined_the_issue: Earlier judgments involving the parties or their predecessors had already determined the same issue.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a concurrent finding is not reopened when the issue is mixed law and fact, was conceded below, and had also been determined in prior judgments.
